source.title: Per-example gradient regularization improves learning signals from noisy data
source.authors: Xuran Meng; Yuan Cao; Difan Zou

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some equations and figure contents are flattened, so exact plotted values cannot be recovered.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests how training procedures affect memorization of noise and test performance in an over-parameterized CNN setting. It does not test the claim versions’ specific interventions or comparisons.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on synthetic signal-plus-noise data and noisy MNIST, comparing per-example gradient regularization (PEGR), full gradient regularization (FGR), and standard training. These bear on generalization under noisy natural labels, but do not test arbitrary random-label fitting, width sweeps, architecture comparisons, optimizer comparisons, batch-size effects, dropout, sharpness measures, or removal of memorized examples.
record.test_reason: The study tests PEGR's effects on learning signals amid input noise, which none of V1–V8 names. It does not compare fitting arbitrary labels with generalizing on natural labels: its synthetic labels determine the signal patch yμ, despite being sampled randomly. Gradient regularization is also not a measurement of magnitude-aware sharpness or its correlation with generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate within the studied conditions: early PEGR suppresses noise memorization while allowing signal learning, and switching it off at an appropriate time permits low training loss and low test error. Standard gradient descent instead memorizes noise and has near-chance test performance under the theoretical low-SNR assumptions. The experiments support the proposed mechanism; the MNIST evaluation uses clean test inputs.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses per-example gradient regularization and a theoretical signal-noise CNN model, rather than random-label fitting/generalization comparisons or the mapped versions’ interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with noise level σp; at σp = 0.1 all synthetic-data methods tend to test accuracy 1, while the text says PEGR alone tends to 1 at the other tested σp values. On MNIST, PEGR is reported to have higher test accuracy under the tested noise levels; test data are kept noise-free.

fits_no_version.finding: Under Condition 3.1, early PEGR followed by unregularized training permits arbitrarily small training loss with test error at most 1/poly(n); unregularized training permits arbitrarily small training loss with test error at least 1/2.01.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early PEGR can separate signal learning from noise memorization and improve generalization in the specified low-SNR two-layer CNN model.

fits_no_version.finding: Synthetic experiments report training losses converging to zero for all methods. PEGR test accuracy tends to 1 at all tested noise levels; all methods tend to 1 at σp=0.1, while FGR and standard training do not achieve this across the other noise settings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: PEGR's generalization advantage over FGR and standard training depends on the signal-to-noise regime in this synthetic setup.

fits_no_version.finding: For LeNet-5 on MNIST with input noise added during training and clean test inputs, the authors report higher test accuracy with PEGR at the tested positive noise levels. They report preserved signal learning without added noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early PEGR improves clean-test accuracy when MNIST training inputs contain substantial noise.

record.problems: The synthetic results use a small network and dataset (width m = 10, training data size n = 20); exact plotted values and uncertainty estimates are not stated in the text. The real-data experiment uses MNIST with noise added to training data while test data remain noise-free, so it does not evaluate same-distribution noisy test examples. The main theoretical results rely on restrictive assumptions for a two-layer CNN with square ReLU activation and fixed second-layer parameters.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Figure values are retained as figure only because the supplied text does not provide recoverable exact values.

untested.parts: No fixed arbitrary-label fitting condition or matched natural-label versus random-label generalization comparison.
No widening experiment beyond the width needed for zero training error.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison or intervention on local connectivity.
No adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparison or tuning-budget comparison.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets or adapted recipes.
No magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation measure, ranking of generalization gaps, or comparison with norm and margin measures.
No influence-based identification and removal of memorized examples followed by retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The own-method performance comparisons belong under fits_no_version rather than as evidence rows for V1–V8. All row states are cannot_determine relative to these versions, not judgments that the reported PEGR effects are unreadable. Citations to batch-size and sharpness findings are background only.

versions.untested_parts: No arbitrary or random-label fitting condition is tested, and the paper does not compare natural-label generalization with random-label test accuracy.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks.
